profile.title: Preparation-Stage Prediabetes Counseling in a Stoic Patient with Night-Eating Pattern and Food/Transportation Barriers
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a patient-centered nutrition assessment with a stoic, low-health-literacy patient in the Preparation stage of change for newly flagged prediabetes and obesity. It emphasizes eliciting an honest 24-hour recall despite minimizing answers, gently uncovering financial and transportation barriers behind a reported-versus-actual adherence mismatch (B12 appointments, intentional meal-skipping), and negotiating a single small, sustainable first step using motivational interviewing, with ADIME documentation.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Newark, New Jersey, on her lunch break before an evening shift

patient.name: Lesli Armstrong
patient.occupation: Part-time receptionist at a dental office
patient.appearance: Calling from her small apartment kitchen on a break, still in her dental-office polo shirt; sits upright but with a visible mild shoulder/waistline asymmetry from longstanding scoliosis; looks tired around the eyes; keeps answers short and polite, arms sometimes crossed, glancing at the clock as if mindful of time.

persona.personality: Stoic, matter-of-fact, prides herself on not complaining or being a burden; private about money and personal struggle; warms up once she feels safe and not judged
persona.communicationStyle: Gives short, minimizing answers at first; deflects or changes subject when money, transportation, or coping comes up; uses plain everyday language, gets confused by medical/lab terms; opens up with concrete, homely phrases once rapport builds
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious under a calm surface; wants to 'do something' about her blood sugar but feels overwhelmed by jargon and doesn't want a long list of changes; glances at the clock, mindful of her lunch break
persona.background: Lesli has worked the front desk at the same Newark dental office for about seven years and knows the regular patients by name. She grew up in a working-class Newark household where you didn't make a fuss about aches and pains, and that stuck with her. She's attended a small Baptist congregation for over a decade; Wednesday potluck and prayer group are the fixed, trusted points of her week. She lives with one roommate who works nights, so they rarely eat together. She keeps a little devotional book in her purse for bus rides and reads it to pass the time.
speechExamples: It's really not that much, I just eat dinner late, that's all.
I don't know, I never really measured it out or anything.
So is that the diabetes or not? I get confused.
As long as it's not shots every day, I guess I'm okay.
Some weeks it's rent or real food, so... yeah.
I don't want a whole plan, just tell me one thing to start.
concerns: Worried the prediabetes will get worse and she'll end up on daily medication like her aunt
Doesn't want to be seen as a burden, including by her church friends
Embarrassed she doesn't really understand what the HbA1c number means
Wants to keep enough energy to get through her double shifts without crashing

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit. Your patient is Lesli Armstrong, a 43-year-old woman recently flagged with prediabetes and obesity at her last wellness checkup. She is calling from home on her lunch break before an evening shift at the dental office where she works part-time. She wants help understanding what's going on with her blood sugar and is hoping for one clear first step. Review her chart before the call.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit after being told her blood sugar is 'a little high'; wants one clear first step to keep it from getting worse
scenario.openingLine: Hi, yeah, so they told me at my last checkup my sugar's a little high. I don't really have a lot of time today, but I figured I'd see what you all think I should do.
tasks: Take a focused 24-hour diet and meal-pattern history, including fluids and timing of meals
Review relevant anthropometrics, vital signs, and laboratory results and relate them to her nutrition status in plain language
Explore barriers to consistent eating, medication adherence, and appointment attendance using non-judgmental, open-ended questions
Assess her understanding of her diagnosis and correct any gaps in plain, low-literacy-friendly language
Negotiate one small, specific, sustainable first-step change consistent with her stated readiness, and document the visit in ADIME format

actions.name: 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: black coffee on waking; nothing at lunch most days; dinner around 9-10 PM after shift consisting of fried chicken or a frozen entrée (Salisbury steak/lasagna) with white rice and gravy; sweet tea and soda through the day; saltine crackers with peanut butter some nights before bed. Denies regular daytime snacking.

actions.name: Usual meal pattern and timing assessment
actions.result: Patient describes a consistent pattern of skipping breakfast and lunch, with one large meal 9-10 PM, roughly a 14-hour gap between the prior night's dinner and the next evening's meal. States this is because she 'loses track of time' during shifts, not an intentional choice.

actions.name: Hunger/satiety and symptom pattern screen
actions.result: Patient reports feeling shaky and very hungry by the end of her shift, low energy in the afternoons, and trouble falling asleep after her late dinner, sleeping about 6-7 hours with some restlessness.

actions.name: Fluid and beverage intake assessment
actions.result: Patient reports sweet tea and a couple of cans of soda most days as her main fluids, says she 'forgets' to drink water, minimal plain water intake reported.

actions.name: Physical activity level assessment
actions.result: Patient reports mostly sedentary days, standing and walking short distances at the front desk, no structured exercise.

actions.name: Weight history and trend review
actions.result: No prior documented weights available for comparison before 2024; current weight 85.3 kg consistent with chart.

actions.name: Review B12 injection appointment/adherence record
actions.result: Clinic scheduling record shows four missed monthly B12 injection appointments in the past 12 months, three of which are annotated 'rescheduled - transportation.' Patient had reported only missing 'one or two' appointments when asked directly.

actions.name: Review grocery/food budget self-report log
actions.result: No structured food budget log on file; information available only through patient interview.

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage of change assessment
actions.result: Patient states she has already decided she wants to work on her blood sugar and is asking for one specific, manageable first step rather than a full overhaul, consistent with the Preparation stage.

actions.name: Health literacy / understanding of diagnosis check
actions.result: Patient states she was told her 'sugar is a little high' but is unsure what HbA1c means or whether prediabetes is 'the diabetes,' and is unclear why she needs the monthly B12 injection beyond 'the doctor said my levels were low.'

objectives.text: Elicit an accurate 24-hour diet and meal-pattern history, including fluid intake and timing, despite the patient's tendency to minimize and give short answers.

Relate anthropometric, vital sign, and laboratory findings to the patient's nutrition status and explain HbA1c/prediabetes in plain, low-health-literacy-friendly language, correcting her confusion with diabetes requiring daily injections.
Explore financial, transportation, and appointment-adherence barriers to consistent eating and medication access using non-judgmental, open-ended questioning.
Assess readiness to change and negotiate one small, specific, sustainable first-step change consistent with the patient's stated preference for a single manageable step rather than a full overhaul.
Identify the patient's faith community as a potential support for behavior change while respecting her reluctance to disclose her diagnosis to church friends.
Elicit pertinent negatives and relevant medical/psychosocial history (hyperglycemia symptoms, family history, reproductive history, substance use) to complete a focused nutrition-relevant history.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Prediabetes with disordered meal timing (prolonged daytime fasting / night-eating pattern) in the context of obesity, food insecurity, and transportation barriers
differential: Excessive caloric intake concentrated in evening meal contributing to impaired glucose metabolism (primary nutrition diagnosis)
Inadequate fluid intake / excess sugar-sweetened beverage intake
Food- and medication-access limitations related to financial resources
Mismatch between reported and actual adherence to recommended follow-up (B12 appointments) suggesting broader pattern of under-reporting barriers
Low health literacy regarding diagnosis and lab values affecting self-management capacity
keyFindings: HbA1c 6.4% (2024-12-10) consistent with prediabetes; fasting glucose 85.4 mg/dL same date
BMI 30.6 kg/m2 (height 167.1 cm, weight 85.3 kg) consistent with obesity
BP 130/92 mmHg today, patient attributes to 'white coat stuff'
Dietary pattern: no breakfast or lunch most days, one large meal ~9-10pm; primary beverages sweet tea/soda, minimal water
Reports shakiness and extreme hunger by end of workday, afternoon low energy, restless sleep after late meal

States she 'always makes' B12 shots and only occasionally runs low on groceries; record/history reveals more frequent missed B12 appointments tied to transportation and a pattern of stretching food budget by skipping meals on purpose, not just losing track of time
Has not disclosed prediabetes diagnosis to her church community despite potluck being a weekly predictable food event
In Preparation stage of change; wants one small, concrete first step rather than a full plan
plan: Document nutrition assessment in ADIME format: diet history (24-hr recall), anthropometrics, relevant labs, psychosocial/financial barriers
Provide plain-language explanation of HbA1c and prediabetes distinct from diabetes, addressing her fear of daily injections
Explore cost and transportation barriers to food and medication access using non-judgmental, open-ended questioning
Negotiate and agree on one small, specific, sustainable first step tied to her existing routine (e.g., a modest daytime snack during work break, or shifting part of her evening meal earlier)
Discuss hydration swap (water or unsweetened option in place of some sweet tea/soda) as a secondary low-burden suggestion only if she has bandwidth
Explore potential to leverage the Wednesday potluck constructively without requiring disclosure of her diagnosis to her church friends
Arrange follow-up nutrition visit to reassess adherence to the agreed first step and revisit barriers
Communicate with referring clinician/team as appropriate regarding missed B12 appointments and transportation barrier (per scope of practice)
redFlags: Elevated BP (130/92) today warrants documentation and routine follow-up with medical provider, not dismissal as isolated white-coat effect
Pattern of skipping meals specifically to stretch grocery budget indicates food insecurity requiring resource referral (e.g., food assistance, social work)

Missed medication/appointment pattern tied to transportation and cost tradeoffs (including the unrelated allergy medication) suggests broader access barriers beyond nutrition that may need interdisciplinary follow-up
educationPoints: Prediabetes is a reversible stage, distinct from diabetes; consistent small changes can reduce progression risk and this does not necessarily lead to insulin or daily injections
Prolonged daytime fasting followed by one large nighttime meal can contribute to blood sugar swings, hunger/shakiness, and poor sleep; spreading intake more evenly can help
Sweet tea and soda contribute meaningful sugar intake even without 'snacking'; small swaps can add up without a full diet overhaul
One small, concrete, sustainable change (not a complete overhaul) fits her stated readiness and routine, and is more likely to succeed than a long list
Existing supports (church potluck, work breaks) can be used as practical anchors for change without requiring her to disclose her diagnosis to others

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports attending her B12 injection appointments consistently (h24)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Clinic scheduling record shows four missed monthly B12 injection appointments in the past 12 months, three annotated 'rescheduled - transportation' (d4, a12)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients, especially stoic ones who downplay struggles, may initially minimize missed appointments; reviewing adherence records alongside the interview can reveal transportation and access barriers that need gentle, non-judgmental exploration rather than confrontation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Initially attributes skipped breakfast and lunch to losing track of time during busy shifts rather than intentional restriction (h7, s15)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Wellness Visit Note documents prediabetes and obesity flag in the context of a dietary pattern consistent with prolonged daytime fasting; with rapport the patient admits meals are sometimes skipped intentionally to stretch her grocery budget (h8, s16)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Initial framing of a behavior as unintentional ('losing track of time') may mask an underlying food-insecurity-driven coping strategy; building rapport before probing financial barriers is essential to surface the true driver of the eating pattern and identify an appropriate nutrition diagnosis and intervention.
